questionText: Elena is extremely proud of the fact that her department has never missed a deadline.
targetSentence: Elena ____ her department's unbroken record of meeting deadlines.
explanation: 'Take pride in' is the fixed collocation; the adjective 'proud' must become the noun after 'take'. Candidates commonly write 'is proud in' or 'takes proud of', mixing the adjectival frame 'proud of' with the nominal one.

questionText: Nobody at the meeting paid any attention to the discrepancy in the accounts.
targetSentence: The discrepancy in the accounts ____ everyone at the meeting.
explanation: The transformation inverts the subject: what people failed to notice becomes the subject of 'escape the notice of'. The usual failure is 'escaped from the notice', since 'escape' in this sense is transitive and takes no preposition.

questionText: It took the new manager months to understand the complexities of the payroll system.
targetSentence: It took the new manager months to ____ the complexities of the payroll system.
explanation: Both 'come to' and 'get to grips with' are current, and the plural 'grips' is invariable. Candidates regularly produce the singular 'grip', which belongs to the unrelated 'get a grip on yourself'.

questionText: After three sleepless nights with the baby, Sara had absolutely no patience left.
targetSentence: After three sleepless nights with the baby, Sara was ____.
explanation: 'At one's wits' end' is a fixed predicative phrase requiring the possessive determiner to agree with the subject. The frequent error is the singular 'wit', which changes the idiom into a comment on humour.

questionText: By the last week of the strike the negotiators had no patience or resolve remaining.
targetSentence: By the last week of the strike the negotiators were ____.
correctAnswer: at the end of their tether
explanation: 'At the end of one's tether' is fixed and the possessive must agree with the plural subject. Learners often reduce it to 'at the tether end' or substitute 'rope', which is the American variant and reads oddly in a British C2 paper.

questionText: The two departments have been in constant disagreement about the budget for months.
targetSentence: The two departments have ____ the budget for months.
explanation: 'At loggerheads' takes 'over' or 'with' but never 'about', so the preposition of the lead sentence cannot simply be carried across. The noun has no singular in this idiom.

questionText: Julián will happily change his plans without a moment's hesitation.
targetSentence: Julián will happily change his plans ____.
correctAnswer: at the drop of a hat
explanation: The idiom is frozen: 'at the drop of a hat', with the indefinite article obligatory. Candidates often write 'at the drop of the hat' or 'in the drop of a hat', both of which are marked wrong.

questionText: The announcement of the merger came as a complete surprise to the entire workforce.
targetSentence: The announcement of the merger came ____ to the entire workforce.
explanation: 'Out of the blue' is adverbial and needs no noun after it, which is what makes it hard to retrieve. The common error is 'out of the blue sky', an over-literal expansion that breaks the fixed phrase.

questionText: When the sponsor withdrew, the organisers were abandoned without any support whatsoever.
targetSentence: When the sponsor withdrew, the organisers ____.
explanation: The passive is required because the organisers are the affected party, and 'lurch' occurs in no other modern context. Candidates who keep the active 'left the organisers in the lurch' lose the subject the target sentence has already fixed.

questionText: Management deliberately gave the staff no information at all about the restructuring.
targetSentence: Management deliberately ____ the restructuring.
correctAnswer: kept the staff in the dark about
explanation: 'Keep someone in the dark about something' needs both the object and the preposition, since the target sentence supplies neither. Learners frequently drop 'about' and produce an ungrammatical string before the noun phrase.

questionText: Please make sure I am told about any developments while I am away next week.
targetSentence: Please make sure you ____ about any developments while I am away next week.
explanation: 'Keep someone in the loop' is the fixed frame; the definite article is obligatory. The usual slip is 'in loop' or 'on the loop', the latter borrowed from 'on the list'.

questionText: Summarised very briefly indeed, the argument is that the whole policy has failed.
targetSentence: ____, the argument is that the whole policy has failed.
explanation: 'In a nutshell' is a sentence adverbial that replaces a whole participial clause, and it takes the indefinite article. Candidates commonly write 'In the nutshell' on the model of 'in the end'.

questionText: I did not follow every word, but I understood the general sense of her argument.
targetSentence: I did not follow every word, but I ____ her argument.
explanation: 'The gist' is always definite and always followed by 'of'. Learners often omit the article, producing 'got gist of', or select 'catch', which collocates with 'drift' rather than 'gist'.

questionText: It took Pau a fortnight to become genuinely competent at using the new software.
targetSentence: It took Pau a fortnight to ____ the new software.
explanation: 'Get the hang of' is fixed with the definite article and 'of'. The verb cannot be varied to 'take' or 'catch', and the noun has no plural in this use.

questionText: Ana is remarkably good at putting nervous candidates at their ease.
targetSentence: Ana ____ putting nervous candidates at their ease.
explanation: 'Have a knack for' takes the indefinite article and is followed by a gerund, which the target sentence already supplies. Candidates often write 'has knack in', losing both the article and the preposition.

questionText: The director has always been rather fond of extremely long takes.
targetSentence: The director has always ____ extremely long takes.
explanation: 'Have a penchant for' is the fixed frame, and the perfect 'has always had' is forced by the adverb already in the target sentence. The preposition is 'for', never 'to' or 'of'.

questionText: Marc strongly dislikes being photographed at social occasions.
targetSentence: Marc ____ being photographed at social occasions.
explanation: 'Aversion' takes 'to', not 'of' or 'for', and the following gerund is already in place. Spanish 'aversión a' happens to agree, but learners still default to 'aversion of' by analogy with 'fear of'.

questionText: The old professor was always rather indulgent towards students who argued with him.
targetSentence: The old professor always ____ students who argued with him.
explanation: 'Have a soft spot for' is fixed, with 'for' rather than 'towards' despite the lead sentence. The noun 'spot' cannot be pluralised even when the object is plural.

questionText: The inspectors deliberately ignored the safety violations for years on end.
targetSentence: The inspectors deliberately ____ the safety violations for years on end.
explanation: The idiom requires the indefinite article and the preposition 'to'; 'eye' stays singular however many things are ignored. Candidates often write 'closed their eyes to', which is a different, weaker expression.

questionText: The council completely ignored the residents' repeated complaints about the noise.
targetSentence: The council ____ the residents' repeated complaints about the noise.
explanation: Parallel to the blind-eye idiom, this one takes 'a deaf ear' in the singular plus 'to'. The frequent error is the plural 'deaf ears', which occurs only in the passive 'fell on deaf ears'.

questionText: Rather than planning anything now, we will decide what to do as the situation develops.
targetSentence: Rather than planning anything now, we will ____ as the situation develops.
explanation: 'Play it by ear' keeps the dummy object 'it', which candidates routinely delete, and takes no article before 'ear'. The idiom is intransitive in effect, so nothing may follow it.

questionText: I know the author's name perfectly well but simply cannot bring it to mind.
targetSentence: The author's name is ____ but I simply cannot bring it to mind.
correctAnswer: on the tip of my tongue
explanation: The idiom is locative and needs both definite articles plus the possessive determiner. Learners frequently omit 'the' before 'tip' or use 'in' instead of 'on'.

questionText: Diego said something tactless and caused considerable embarrassment at dinner.
targetSentence: Diego really ____ at dinner.
correctAnswer: put his foot in his mouth
explanation: Both variants are current, and both keep 'foot' singular. The commonest error is the plural 'put his feet in it', which destroys the idiom entirely.

questionText: Her parents ended up paying for the entire wedding themselves.
targetSentence: Her parents ended up ____ the entire wedding themselves.
explanation: 'Foot the bill' is the fixed verb-noun pair, and 'for' is needed before the thing paid for. The gerund is forced by 'ended up', and candidates often supply the infinitive instead.

questionText: After a disastrous first half, the home side completely reversed the situation.
targetSentence: After a disastrous first half, the home side ____ their opponents.
explanation: 'Turn the tables on someone' requires the plural noun and the preposition 'on'. Candidates writing 'turned the table' or 'turned the tables against' lose the mark on a single word.
